Yes, for any commit that gets replayed. A commit's hash covers its parent hash, tree, author, committer, and message. Rebasing gives a commit a new parent, and the committer timestamp is updated, so the hash changes. Every descendant of a changed commit changes too.

Commits that aren't replayed keep their hashes: those at or before the new base, and any that git skips as already applied. If the rebase is a no-op, such as a fast-forward onto the same base, nothing changes.

This is why rebasing commits you've already pushed requires a force-push and disrupts anyone who based work on the old hashes.
